items.question: When budgeting a request, why must an architect reserve headroom beyond the size of the assembled input?

options.A: The reply is generated into the same window, so an input that only just fits leaves no room for a complete answer.
options.B: The provider holds back a fixed fraction of the advertised window for internal use, and that portion is never available to the caller.
options.C: Tokenisation of an assembled prompt is non-deterministic, so the true count on the server can exceed whatever the caller estimated locally.
options.D: Headroom is needed so that a retry following a transient error can re-send the request with additional diagnostic context attached.

items.question: An agritech firm's advisory assistant answers agronomist questions from a 90-document crop-protocol library that fits comfortably in the window, and the team loads the whole library on every request. Broad synthesising questions are answered excellently. Narrow ones — the re-entry interval for a specific product on a specific crop — are inconsistent and sometimes cite the wrong crop. Cost per request is high. What should change?

options.A: Reorder the library so that the most frequently queried protocols appear first, where they will be attended to most reliably.
options.B: Continue loading the whole library, but require the assistant to quote the exact protocol section it is relying on before it gives any answer to the agronomist.
options.C: Add a retrieval step so narrow questions are answered from the few relevant sections, and keep whole-library loading for the synthesising questions.
options.D: Split the library across two calls of roughly equal size and merge the two answers into a single response.

items.question: A retailer refactored its merchandising agent so each of five product categories is analysed by its own sub-agent, specifically to keep the orchestrator's window clean. Total token spend tripled and end-to-end latency roughly doubled, while answer quality is unchanged. All five analyses need the same three reference documents: the pricing policy, the current promotional calendar and the category taxonomy. What went wrong?

options.A: The shared reference documents are loaded five times over, so isolation duplicated the bulk of the context instead of reducing it.
options.B: The sub-agents should be run sequentially rather than in parallel, so that each can reuse the previous one's findings and avoid redundant analysis.
options.C: The orchestrator's schema for sub-agent returns is too permissive, allowing each worker to return far more material than the orchestrator needs.
options.D: The five product categories are too coarse a decomposition, and splitting them further would give each sub-agent a smaller and more tractable slice.

items.question: As a context strategy, what does progressive disclosure mean?

options.A: Revealing the agent's intermediate reasoning to the end user in stages, so they can follow how a conclusion was reached.
options.B: Exposing a high-level index first and loading detail only for the parts the agent selects.
options.C: Raising the context budget gradually across a conversation as it demonstrates that the extra material is being used well.
options.D: Releasing a new prompt version to a small share of production traffic before rolling it out to everyone.

items.question: An education platform lets tutors edit an earlier message in a conversation with the lesson-planning assistant and regenerate from that point. The team is deciding how to manage conversation state. Which TWO statements about this design are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The stored conversation has to be a tree or a versioned list, because an edit creates a branch rather than an append.
options.B: An edit can be applied by appending a correction turn at the end, which is functionally equivalent to editing the message in place.
options.C: Everything after the edited turn must be dropped from the prompt, because it was produced in response to text that no longer exists.
options.D: Any summary produced from turns after the edit point stays valid, since summarisation output does not depend on the turns that preceded it.
options.E: Because only a single turn changed, the rest of the request is unaffected and the assembled prompt remains reusable end to end.

items.question: A food-delivery platform's order-support assistant carries the full chat transcript. Complaints centre on it quoting an order status that was true twenty minutes earlier: the status arrived in a tool result early in the conversation and has stayed in the window ever since. Timestamps were added to every tool result last quarter, which reduced but did not eliminate the problem. What is the right correction?

options.A: Compact the transcript more aggressively, so that older tool results are summarised away sooner in the conversation.
options.B: Make the timestamp more prominent by moving it onto a header line above each tool result rather than leaving it inline.
options.C: Add a system-prompt instruction telling the assistant never to rely on a tool result from an earlier turn of the conversation.
options.D: Classify tool results by durability and strip volatile ones from the transcript once superseded, refetching status on demand.

items.question: A mining company's plant-diagnostics agent investigates equipment faults from operational logs. It currently pulls the last 24 hours of logs for the affected asset — often hundreds of thousands of lines — into context and then reasons over them. Most investigations turn on a handful of lines. Runs are slow, expensive, and the agent frequently overlooks the relevant entries. The log store supports pattern search with time filters. What should the team do next?

options.A: Expose the log store's search as a tool and have the agent iterate: search for candidate patterns, then read only the surrounding window around each match.
options.B: Pre-summarise each hour of logs into a digest and load the twenty-four digests instead of the raw lines.
options.C: Narrow the retrieval window from twenty-four hours down to two hours around the reported fault time.
options.D: Move the diagnostics agent onto a capability tier with demonstrably stronger recall over long inputs, and keep the existing twenty-four-hour loading strategy unchanged.

items.question: A long-running agent compacts repeatedly, and each pass summarises a context that already contains the output of previous passes. What is the characteristic risk?

options.A: The summary lengthens with every pass, because the model tries to preserve everything it is shown and never discards enough.
options.B: Detail is lost irreversibly and small distortions compound, because each pass has only the previous summary as its source.
options.C: Latency grows with each pass, because the summariser is handed progressively more input than the pass before it.
options.D: The summary starts to contradict the system prompt, because the standing instructions get re-paraphrased along with the conversation.

items.question: A gaming company's support assistant handles players who return weeks apart, and product wants it to remember past tickets. An engineer proposes concatenating every previous conversation with that player into the window at session start. Sessions are typically short and most players have a long history. What is the sounder design?

options.A: Maintain a durable player profile of resolved issues, entitlements and preferences, load it at session start, and retrieve a full past transcript only when the current session refers to one.
options.B: Concatenate only the five most recent conversations, which bounds the growth of the session-start payload while keeping the assistant reasonably well informed about the player's recent history with support.
options.C: Regenerate a single running player summary at the end of every session from that player's complete conversation history to date.
options.D: Keep loading the entire history and rely on compaction to bring the assembled context back within the window.

items.question: A pharmaceutical company's regulatory-writing assistant drafts sections of a submission dossier over long sessions, compacting as the session grows. QA has found that extracts from the approved product label, which must appear word-for-word, are subtly reworded in later drafts — the compaction paraphrased them. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Instruct the summariser to reproduce any quoted material exactly and never to rephrase text that appears inside quotation marks.
options.B: Have QA diff the finished draft against the approved label and correct any wording that has drifted before submission.
options.C: Hold protected extracts outside the compacted transcript in a pinned block, referenced by identifier when the drafting step needs them.
options.D: Disable compaction for regulatory sessions so that the original extracts remain in the window for the whole drafting run.

items.question: Why should a context-assembly step emit its blocks in a deterministic order?

options.A: Non-deterministic ordering makes the prefix differ between otherwise identical requests, destroying reuse and making failures hard to reproduce.
options.B: The model needs blocks in a fixed sequence in order to parse XML delimiters correctly and associate closing tags with their openers.
options.C: Ordering determines which block the model treats as authoritative, so a fixed order guarantees the system prompt wins any instruction conflict.
options.D: A deterministic order is what allows the assembly step to guarantee that the finished prompt will fit inside the context window.

items.question: An automotive dealer group's sales assistant assembles a context brief at the start of each customer session. Sessions are short, the CRM is large, and the assistant already has read access to the CRM through tools. Which TWO items belong in the brief itself rather than behind a tool call? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The group's full new and used vehicle inventory, so availability questions can be answered without a round trip to the CRM.
options.B: The customer's current open enquiry and the vehicle it concerns.
options.C: The customer's complete service history across every vehicle they have owned from the group.
options.D: The customer's finance pre-approval status and its expiry date, which gate what the assistant may offer at all.
options.E: The full text of the group's warranty terms, so that any wording the assistant quotes is exact.

items.question: An airline's irregular-operations assistant must reason over crew rosters, aircraft rotations, passenger connections and maintenance holds during a disruption. Each dataset is large and together they exceed the window. The four analyses are largely independent, but the final recommendation has to trade them off against one another. Duty controllers need an answer within a few minutes. Which shape fits?

options.A: Four workers, each with its own window and dataset, returning a bounded structured assessment to an orchestrator that sees only those four assessments and makes the trade-off.
options.B: One agent that loads each of the four datasets in turn and summarises as it goes, so that by the end of the sequence it is holding a single condensed view of all four datasets together.
options.C: A retrieval layer spanning all four datasets, with a single agent issuing queries across them as the disruption analysis proceeds.
options.D: Four sequential calls, each carrying the previous calls' outputs forward, with the final call producing the overall recommendation.

items.question: Retrieved passages are placed in the window each with a short header giving source document, section and date. What does that header primarily buy?

options.A: Better retrieval recall, because the embedding model has more signal to work with when it scores candidate passages.
options.B: A reduction in the tokens the passages consume, because the header replaces repeated context inside the passage body.
options.C: Protection against retrieved text being read as instruction, because headers mark the boundary of untrusted content.
options.D: The ability to attribute claims and to weigh conflicting passages by recency or source authority.

items.question: A construction firm's permitting assistant handles applications that run over several days. Users report that it asks them to re-supply the site address and parcel number they already provided, and it happens after long gaps in the conversation. Logs confirm the conversation record is intact across those gaps and that compaction fired during each one. What is the defect?

options.A: The conversation store is dropping turns during idle periods, so the earlier exchanges are genuinely absent when the user returns.
options.B: The system prompt does not instruct the assistant to retain and reuse facts the user has already supplied during the application.
options.C: The compaction summary preserves the narrative of the conversation but drops the structured facts the workflow depends on.
options.D: Users are starting fresh conversations after the gap rather than resuming the existing one, so the assistant has no prior context.

items.question: In context engineering, what does an agent's "working set" refer to?

options.A: The maximum number of tokens the model will accept in a single request, as published in the specification for that model version.
options.B: The subset of the available information that the agent actually needs resident in order to complete its current step.
options.C: The collection of tools the agent has been granted permission to call for the duration of the session.
options.D: The number of tokens already consumed by the conversation up to the current point in the run.

items.question: A wealth manager's advice-drafting assistant produces suitability notes. The regulator requires the firm to show, for any note, exactly which client facts and which product documents informed it, for six years after issue. Today context is assembled dynamically from a CRM and a product library, and the team logs only the final note and the adviser's prompt. An audit request has just arrived covering notes from eighteen months ago. What should the team do next?

options.A: Re-run the assistant against the current CRM and product library to reproduce each note under audit and show how it was derived.
options.B: Log the model version and sampling parameters going forward, so that any note can be regenerated deterministically on demand.
options.C: Ask the CRM and product library owners to supply their full change histories covering the audit period, so that the inputs to each note can be inferred retrospectively.
options.D: Persist, alongside each note, either the fully assembled prompt or a manifest naming every context block with its source identifier and version.

items.question: A broadcaster runs summarisation in two places: an interactive newsroom tool with a sub-second expectation, and an overnight batch over the day's wire feed. An architect argues the two should use different context strategies. Which TWO of the proposed differences are justified? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The batch path should be configured with a larger context window than the interactive path, since it has no latency constraint to respect.
options.B: The batch path can afford multi-pass processing — mapping over sections then reducing — where the interactive path must answer in a single call.
options.C: The interactive path should skip retrieval entirely, because a retrieval hop always breaches a sub-second budget.
options.D: The interactive path benefits more from a stable shared prefix, because it issues many similar requests in quick succession.
options.E: The batch path should disable compaction, since compaction exists to reduce latency and there is no latency pressure overnight.

items.question: Beyond the wasted tokens, why is it a problem when the same document appears twice in a request's context?

options.A: Duplicate blocks are rejected by the API, so the request fails before the model ever sees it.
options.B: Repetition can be read as emphasis, skewing the model toward that content and away from the material it appears alongside.
options.C: The tokeniser handles the second copy differently, so its content is encoded less accurately than the first.
options.D: Duplicates prevent the request from reusing a prefix, because the assembled prompt is no longer byte-identical to earlier ones.

items.question: A pension provider's member-services assistant has a system prompt that has grown over two years as each production incident added a rule for the case that caused it. It now runs to several hundred lines. New rules increasingly fail to take effect, and fixing one regression tends to reintroduce another. What is the right restructuring?

options.A: Keep a compact core of rules that apply to every request, and attach case-specific guidance conditionally, triggered by the request classification it belongs to.
options.B: Reorder the accumulated rules so that the most recently added ones appear at the very end of the prompt, where they are most likely to be attended to on any given request.
options.C: Convert the rule list into a numbered checklist that the assistant is required to walk through explicitly before it produces its reply.
options.D: Move the whole rule set into a retrieved document and fetch it at the start of every request rather than embedding it in the prompt.

items.question: A port operator's berth-scheduling agent replans whenever a vessel's ETA moves, which during bad weather can be every few minutes. Each replan writes a full plan into the transcript. By the end of a shift the context is mostly obsolete plans, the agent has begun blending elements of superseded plans into new ones, and controllers no longer trust its output. What is the right change?

options.A: Cap the number of replans permitted per shift and require controller approval beyond that cap.
options.B: Keep only the current plan in the transcript, writing superseded plans to a durable history the agent can consult when it needs to explain a change.
options.C: Have the agent emit only the delta from the previous plan on each replan, rather than reproducing the entire berth schedule in full every time an ETA moves.
options.D: Compact the accumulated plans periodically into a summary of how the schedule has evolved during the shift.

items.question: A team has introduced just-in-time loading in place of bulk preloading. Which single measurement most directly tells them whether the new strategy is doing its job?

options.A: Total tokens consumed per day across the service, compared against the same period before the change was deployed.
options.B: The proportion of loaded content that the model's answer actually drew on, tracked per request alongside answer quality.
options.C: Peak context utilisation on the largest request seen each day, since that is the request closest to the ceiling.
options.D: The number of tool calls per request, which shows how often the agent is choosing to fetch content on demand.

items.question: A hospital group's theatre-scheduling assistant currently loads its whole policy and rota corpus into the window on every request. An architect is assessing whether to move to retrieval. Which TWO observations would most strongly support making that move? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The corpus has grown by half since launch and continues to grow as new specialties are onboarded onto the platform.
options.B: Answer quality is highest on questions that require synthesising several policies at once, and has held steady on narrow lookups since launch.
options.C: Cost per request has risen even though the number of requests per day has stayed flat.
options.D: Clinicians occasionally ask questions the corpus cannot answer at all, and the assistant says so correctly.
options.E: Time to first token has improved since the team moved the corpus to the front of the prompt.

items.question: A telco's dispute-resolution assistant must answer questions about a single enterprise customer's billing history. For the largest accounts, one month of itemised usage alone exceeds the window, and the questions genuinely require the itemised detail rather than a total — for example, identifying every call routed through a particular carrier. Trimming and summarising have both been tried and both lose the detail the answer depends on. What should the team do next?

options.A: Move the filtering out of the model entirely: have a query layer select the matching records, and give the model only the result set to reason about.
options.B: Partition the month into windows that fit, run the same question over each, and combine the per-window answers into a final response.
options.C: Escalate these accounts to a human billing analyst, since the volume of itemised detail on the largest enterprise customers is beyond what the assistant can reasonably handle.
options.D: Compress the itemised records into a denser tabular encoding so that a full month fits inside the window.

items.question: A design replaces unbounded conversation history with a fixed-size rolling summary. What is the principal trade-off being accepted?

options.A: Per-turn cost stops growing with conversation length, at the price of losing detail that the summary had no room to keep.
options.B: Answers become faster but less consistent, because a summary is regenerated differently on each turn of the conversation.
options.C: The system becomes simpler to operate, at the price of no longer being able to show a user what was said earlier.
options.D: Accuracy improves on recent turns, at the price of the model losing access to the standing instructions in the system prompt.

items.question: An aerospace supplier's engineering assistant supports long design conversations. Engineers routinely paste a full test report — sometimes tens of thousands of tokens — into the middle of a thread, ask two questions about it, and then move on to other topics. The report stays in the transcript for the rest of the session and squeezes out later work. What is the right handling?

options.A: Reject pastes above a size threshold and require the engineer to attach the report as a file instead of inlining it.
options.B: Ingest large pastes as addressable attachments, keep a short reference in the transcript, and load the full text only for turns that need it.
options.C: Summarise the report immediately on paste and keep only the summary in the transcript for the remainder of the session.
options.D: Let the report stay in the transcript and rely on the session's regular compaction pass to remove it once it has stopped being referenced by the engineer.

items.question: A fashion retailer's markdown-planning agent was split into isolated sub-agents, one per region, to control context growth. Each region's decisions consume a shared clearance-inventory pool. The regional plans now regularly commit the same stock twice, and the orchestrator only discovers the conflict when it aggregates at the end. What does this indicate?

options.A: The orchestrator's aggregation step needs a reconciliation pass that detects double-committed stock and reallocates it between the regional plans.
options.B: The regional sub-agents need larger context windows so that each can hold the full clearance inventory alongside its own regional data.
options.C: The sub-agents should be run sequentially, each seeing the commitments made by the regions that ran before it.
options.D: The subtasks share mutable state, so context isolation was the wrong decomposition — allocation belongs in one place rather than in parallel workers.

items.question: A request has been assembled and is over budget. Which remedy should generally be attempted first?

options.A: Compact the conversation history, which is usually the largest single contributor to an oversized request.
options.B: Drop content that is redundant or demonstrably unused before degrading anything the task actually needs.
options.C: Split the work into several calls, since anything over budget is by definition too large for one request.
options.D: Reduce the reserved output allowance, since input content is more likely to be needed than a long reply.

items.question: A grant-making foundation's application-review assistant has started producing summaries that omit the applicant's stated budget. The team has two hypotheses: the instruction that asks for the budget is being missed, or the budget is not reaching the window at all. Which investigation distinguishes them most cheaply?

options.A: Run the same applications through a higher-capability tier and see whether the omissions stop occurring.
options.B: Add a stronger instruction emphasising the budget field and measure whether the omission rate falls in production.
options.C: Log the assembled prompt for failing cases and check whether the budget text is present in it.
options.D: Ask the assistant, in a follow-up turn, whether it saw a budget in the application it just reviewed.

items.question: A rail operator is writing the compaction policy for a long-running incident-management agent before it goes to production. Which THREE elements does the policy need to specify to be operable? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The trigger condition, expressed in measured context utilisation with reserved headroom rather than in turn or tool-call counts.
options.B: The required contents of the summary, naming the fields that must survive and which of them must survive verbatim.
options.C: The maximum number of compactions permitted per incident, after which the run is terminated and handed to a controller.
options.D: What is excluded from the compacted region — the system prompt, pinned reference material and the most recent turns.
options.E: The model tier permitted to serve the agent's own reasoning steps between compactions.

items.question: A publisher's rights-clearance agent maintains a notes file across a long clearance job. The team is deciding which parts of the notes the model writes and which the surrounding code writes. Which division is soundest?

options.A: The model writes everything, since it has the fullest picture of what has happened during the job and can describe it in one place.
options.B: Code writes the objective record — which works were checked, what each tool returned, what time it happened — and the model writes the interpretation and the open questions.
options.C: Code writes everything by extracting fields from the model's replies, so that the notes are never subject to the model's discretion.
options.D: The model writes a free-text draft note after each step and code then rewrites that draft into the schema, so that both the wording and the structure are validated before storage.

items.question: Why should a long-running agent be made to re-read its external notes after a compaction, rather than relying on what remains in the window?

options.A: Because the notes file is the authoritative record and the compacted summary is a lossy derivative of a transcript that may already have diverged from it.
options.B: Because re-reading resets the model's attention over the task, which measurably improves its performance on the several turns immediately following each compaction.
options.C: Because the compaction step cannot access files, so the notes are guaranteed to be missing from the summary it produces.
options.D: Because a file read is cheaper in tokens than the equivalent content held in the transcript across the same number of turns.

items.question: A hotel group's revenue assistant retrieves market and competitor data on most turns and currently appends each turn's passages immediately after the turn that triggered them. Analysts report that in long sessions the assistant increasingly cites data from earlier questions when answering the current one, and that it sometimes treats a superseded figure as current. What structural change addresses this?

options.A: Collect retrieved passages into a single labelled reference section, rebuilt for the current question and placed together rather than scattered through the conversation.
options.B: Keep the interleaved placement but prefix each passage with the turn number it was retrieved for, so the association is explicit.
options.C: Retrieve once at the start of the session using the analyst's stated objective, and reuse that passage set for every subsequent question.
options.D: Move all retrieved passages into the system prompt, where the model will treat them as standing reference material rather than as ordinary conversational content contributed by the analyst.

items.question: A water utility's asset-planning assistant has become unreliable. The team is deciding whether they have a context problem or have outgrown the model's capability. Which TWO observations point specifically at context saturation rather than at a capability ceiling? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Accuracy on a fixed eval set is stable when the inputs are small and falls steadily as input size grows, with no change to the task itself.
options.B: The assistant fails on the same conceptually difficult cases regardless of how much or how little context accompanies them.
options.C: Reordering the prompt so the instructions sit adjacent to the question measurably improves results on the failing cases.
options.D: Failures cluster in the assistant's newest feature area, which was added last month with a new set of rules.
options.E: Answer quality improves when the team moves to the higher-capability tier without changing anything else in the prompt.

items.question: A university's student-services assistant is comfortably inside its context window — utilisation sits around half. But in longer conversations it increasingly answers a previous question rather than the one just asked, and follow-up corrections from the student are frequently ignored. The team has confirmed the newest turn is present and correctly formatted in every request. What should they do next?

options.A: Raise the compaction threshold so that more of the conversation is retained and the assistant has fuller context about the student to work from.
options.B: Restructure the request so the current question is clearly demarcated and positioned last, after the history and any reference material.
options.C: Move to a higher-capability tier, since the assistant is evidently struggling to track the conversation's state.
options.D: Reset the conversation after a set number of turns and ask the student to restate anything still outstanding.

items.question: A semiconductor firm runs three internal assistants — yield analysis, supplier chat and equipment maintenance — from one monolithic system prompt containing every product's rules, so a single team can maintain it. Each product carries the other two's instructions on every request, and cross-product instruction conflicts have caused two incidents. The team is moving to a layered design. Which TWO properties should the new design have? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A shared base layer holding only the rules that genuinely apply to all three products, with product-specific layers composed on top per request.
options.B: Each product should own a complete, independent copy of the prompt, so that no change to one can ever affect another.
options.C: Composition must be deterministic and ordered, so a given product's assembled prompt is byte-identical across requests and reviewable as a versioned artefact.
options.D: The base layer should retain the other products' rules as inactive context, so any assistant can answer a question about a sibling product if asked.
options.E: Product layers should be retrieved at request time from a shared store, so that rule changes take effect without redeploying any of the three assistants.

items.question: A payments processor has 40 engineers using Claude Code across a dozen repositories. After an incident where an agent read a developer's local `.env` file into a transcript, the security team issues a hard requirement: no engineer, on any machine, may configure Claude Code so that it can read environment files or execute infrastructure apply commands. Engineers currently manage their own configuration and several have added broad allow rules for convenience. Which placement of the restriction actually satisfies the requirement?

options.A: Add an explicit prohibition to the root `CLAUDE.md` of every repository, stating in imperative language that the assistant must never open environment files or run infrastructure apply commands.
options.B: Deploy the deny rules through enterprise-managed policy settings distributed by the fleet's device management, and use the same policy to remove the permission mode that skips prompting.
options.C: Ship a one-time onboarding script that writes the deny rules into each engineer's user-level settings file at `~/.claude/settings.json` when they join the team.
options.D: Commit the deny rules to each repository's `.claude/settings.json` and protect that file with a CODEOWNERS rule so changes require security review before merge.

items.question: The same Claude Code settings key is defined in four different places. Which source wins?

options.A: The project's shared settings file at `.claude/settings.json`, because it is the one the whole team agreed on and it is under version control.
options.B: Enterprise-managed policy settings deployed by the organisation.
options.C: The user's personal settings at `~/.claude/settings.json`, because the person at the keyboard is closest to the running session.
options.D: The project-local settings file at `.claude/settings.local.json`, because it is the most specific file and it is written last.

items.question: A logistics platform team wants Claude Code to run their build scripts without prompting, so their shared project settings contain an allow rule matching all `npm run` invocations. A separate rule set, added later by the release engineer, contains a deny rule matching `npm run deploy`. During a session Claude proposes `npm run deploy`. What happens, and why?

options.A: The call runs without prompting, because the allow rule was defined in the higher-precedence settings file and precedence is resolved before rule category.
options.B: The user is prompted to approve or reject, because a rule conflict is treated as an unresolved case and falls back to interactive confirmation.
options.C: The call runs without prompting, because the more general allow rule matched a longer prefix of the command string than the narrower deny rule did.
options.D: The call is refused, because permission rules are evaluated deny first and the first matching rule in that order decides the outcome.

items.question: A telecom operator keeps eleven services in one monorepo. Each service has its own test runner, its own migration conventions, and in two cases a hard rule about never touching generated client code. A staff engineer's first attempt put every service's rules into one root memory file, which grew past a thousand lines and measurably crowded out working context on short tasks. How should the guidance be organised?

options.A: Keep the single root memory file but compress it aggressively into terse bullet points, so all eleven services stay described in a fraction of the tokens.
options.B: Move the service-specific rules into each engineer's user-level memory file, so people only carry the conventions for the services they personally work on.
options.C: Move all eleven rule sets into a single shared wiki page owned by the platform team, and have the root memory file instruct the assistant to fetch that page over the network before it starts any task.
options.D: Keep only repo-wide conventions in the root memory file and put each service's rules in a memory file inside that service's own directory, where they load when work touches that subtree.

items.question: A 40-person platform team is splitting its Claude Code configuration between the repository-committed `.claude/settings.json`, personal files, and organisational policy. Which TWO items belong in the repository-committed project settings file? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The credential the team uses to reach its internal model gateway, stored inline so every clone authenticates identically without extra setup.
options.B: A hook, shared by the whole team, that rejects edits to the directory of generated protocol buffer stubs.
options.C: Deny rules that the security organisation requires to remain in force regardless of what any individual engineer configures on their machine.
options.D: Allow rules covering the repository's own build, lint, and test commands, so that a fresh clone stops prompting for the commands everyone runs constantly.
options.E: One engineer's preferred default model and custom status line, which they have tuned over several months and want applied whenever they open this repository.

items.question: A media company adds a nightly job that runs Claude Code non-interactively to regenerate changelog entries and open a pull request. The runner has a checkout of the repository and a token that can push branches. Nobody watches the job. The first attempt hung until the job timed out. Which permission configuration should the team adopt?

options.A: Leave the default permission mode in place and configure the runner to answer prompts automatically by feeding approvals to standard input as they appear.
options.B: Run in print mode with an explicit allowlist naming only the tools and commands the changelog job needs, executed inside a container that holds nothing beyond the checkout and the push token.
options.C: Enable the mode that skips permission prompts entirely on the runner, since there is no human present to approve anything and the job must not stall again.
options.D: Have each engineer add the necessary allow rules to their own user settings file, so that whichever engineer's configuration the runner inherits already covers the job's needs.

items.question: A script must run Claude Code without a terminal UI and parse the result programmatically. Which invocation is correct?

options.A: Use the resume flag with a stored session identifier, which replays the prior session and emits its transcript in a structured form for the script to read.
options.B: Use the print flag to run non-interactively, together with the output-format option set to a structured format rather than plain text.
options.C: Use the verbose flag, which switches the CLI out of interactive rendering and into a line-delimited structured log suitable for parsing.
options.D: Launch the interactive session normally and capture the terminal output, then strip the rendering escape sequences before parsing the remaining text.

items.question: A fintech team's review queue is clogged with formatting-only diff noise from files Claude Code has edited. The repository has a formatter with a single canonical configuration. The tech lead wants every file the assistant writes to come out formatted, every time, without depending on the model remembering. What should be configured?

options.A: A post-tool-use hook matched to the file-editing tools that runs the formatter against the file that was just written.
options.B: A pre-tool-use hook matched to the file-editing tools that runs the formatter against the target path before the edit is applied.
options.C: A line in the project memory file telling the assistant to run the repository formatter immediately after every file it edits.
options.D: A stop hook that runs the formatter across the whole repository once the assistant finishes responding, catching anything that was left unformatted.

items.question: A hospital group's engineering team uses Claude Code on a records system. De-identified test fixtures are safe to read, but a subset of fixture files carry a classification marker in their header indicating they still contain real patient data, and those files must never enter a model context. The markers are not predictable from filenames or directory layout — they are added by a data-governance job. Approving on a case-by-case basis has already failed once. What mechanism meets the requirement?

options.A: A deny rule listing the fixture paths, regenerated by the governance job each night so the rule set tracks whichever files are currently marked.
options.B: A post-tool-use hook that scans the returned file content for the classification marker and redacts it before the result reaches the model.
options.C: A memory-file rule instructing the assistant to open each fixture's header first and abandon the read if it finds a classification marker.
options.D: A pre-tool-use hook matched to the read tool that inspects the target file's header and returns a deny decision when the marker is present.

items.question: An internal audit at an insurance carrier finds that three of 60 engineers have been launching Claude Code with permission prompting disabled on their laptops, because a slow approval flow was interrupting them. No harm resulted. The engineering director has already agreed to fix the underlying friction by broadening the allow rules for routine build and test commands. What should be done next?

options.A: Publish an acceptable-use note explaining why prompting matters and ask the three engineers to confirm in writing that they have stopped using the mode.
options.B: Deploy an organisational policy setting that removes the prompt-skipping mode from the set of modes a session can select, so the choice is unavailable regardless of local configuration.
options.C: Add deny rules to every repository's shared project settings covering the destructive commands that a session with prompting disabled could otherwise reach.
options.D: Add a monitoring hook to each engineer's user settings that reports the active permission mode to a central endpoint at the start of every session.

items.question: A public-sector delivery team of 25 has built an MCP server that exposes their case-management sandbox. Every engineer working in the main repository should get it, with the same command, arguments, and endpoint, and it should arrive automatically for new joiners and for anyone who clones the repo. The server needs a per-developer access token that must not be committed. How should it be configured?

options.A: Configure it at user scope on each machine, so that it is available in every repository the engineer opens and does not need to be repeated per project.
options.B: Configure it at local scope on the tech lead's machine and export the resulting configuration as a snippet in the team wiki for others to paste in.
options.C: Configure it at project scope so it is written to the repository's `.mcp.json` and committed, with the token supplied through environment-variable expansion rather than a literal value.
options.D: Commit a setup script that each engineer runs once, which adds the server at local scope with their own token baked into the generated configuration.

items.question: A team wants a permission rule that targets one specific tool exposed by an MCP server. How is that tool named in the rule?

options.A: With an `mcp` prefix, then the server name, then the tool name, joined by double underscores.
options.B: With the server's transport type followed by a colon and the tool name, so that stdio and HTTP servers are distinguishable in the rule set.
options.C: With the bare tool name as the server advertises it, since tool names are required to be unique across all connected servers.
options.D: With the absolute path to the server's configuration entry followed by a slash and the tool name, matching how the server was registered.

items.question: A manufacturing software group has a release runbook: 40 steps covering version bumps, signed artefact publication, and a rollback drill. It is used perhaps twice a month, but when it is used the assistant must have the full text and must apply it inside the working tree. Adding it to the project memory file made every unrelated session pay for it in context. The group wants it loaded only when relevant, and available whether an engineer asks for it by name or the assistant recognises a release is under way. What should they build?

options.A: A skill in the repository whose front matter describes when it applies, so only that description is carried until the procedure is actually needed.
options.B: A subagent carrying the runbook in its system prompt, delegated to whenever a release starts, returning its findings to the main session when finished.
options.C: A wrapper script that appends the runbook to the system prompt at launch whenever the engineer passes a release flag to the CLI.
options.D: A pre-compact hook that reinjects the runbook whenever the session compacts, keeping it present in later stages of long release sessions.

items.question: A regulated brokerage is preparing to roll out organisation-managed Claude Code settings to 300 engineers. Which TWO statements about managed policy settings are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: For the same key, a managed value takes precedence over project-local, shared project, and user settings.
options.B: Managed settings are stored in the repository alongside the project settings file so that the team can review policy changes in pull requests.
options.C: A deny rule set by policy is still evaluated ahead of allow rules contributed by any other configuration source.
options.D: An engineer can override a managed value for a single run by passing their own settings file to the CLI on the command line.
options.E: Managed settings govern interactive terminal sessions only; non-interactive print-mode runs resolve configuration from the user's settings instead.

items.question: An energy utility wants to let Claude Code run multi-hour autonomous refactors overnight with minimal prompting. The team accepts that the session will take actions nobody reviewed in advance, and wants to bound what those actions can reach. Which TWO measures actually contain the blast radius? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Raising the default command timeout so long-running builds are not cut short mid-refactor and do not leave the tree in a half-migrated state.
options.B: Recording the prohibition on destructive commands in the project memory file so the model has the constraint in context throughout the run.
options.C: Executing the session inside a container that mounts only the working repository and applies a default-deny outbound network policy.
options.D: Enabling verbose output so an engineer can read the full transcript in the morning and see exactly which commands the session chose to run.
options.E: Adding deny rules for credential paths and destructive commands, which are evaluated ahead of any allow rule the run is operating under.

items.question: A retailer runs a Claude Code step in its release pipeline that generates migration notes. It was stable for months. Last week it began behaving inconsistently between runs: sometimes it produces the expected note, sometimes it times out. Investigation shows a contributor recently added a new MCP server and two hooks to the repository's checked-in configuration, and the pipeline picks up whatever is in the working tree at run time. The pipeline's own requirements have not changed. What is the right next step?

options.A: Ask the contributor to move the new server and hooks into personal configuration so the repository's checked-in configuration returns to what it was when the pipeline was stable.
options.B: Pin the pipeline's model and lower its turn limit, so that whichever configuration is present the step finishes inside the release window rather than timing out.
options.C: Have the pipeline copy the repository's configuration into an artefact at the start of each run, so that when a run misbehaves the exact configuration used can be reconstructed.
options.D: Give the pipeline an explicit configuration of its own — its own settings file and its own MCP configuration, with discovery of repository-supplied servers switched off.

items.question: Which TWO statements about the split between personal and team-shared Claude Code configuration are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Configuration committed in a project's `.claude/settings.json` only takes effect for a teammate after they re-run the CLI installer or clear their session cache.
options.B: The project-local settings file is intended for personal, machine-specific overrides and is kept out of version control.
options.C: A subagent defined in the user's personal agents directory overrides a project-defined subagent that shares its name.
options.D: Settings at `~/.claude/settings.json` apply across every project on that machine and are the lowest-precedence source in the chain.
options.E: Shared credentials belong in the committed project settings file so that every clone authenticates the same way without per-developer setup.

items.question: A repository has a `CLAUDE.md` at its root and the engineer also has one at `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. How are the two treated in a session opened in that repository?

options.A: Only the project file is used, because a project-scoped memory file replaces the user-level one for any session opened inside that project.
options.B: Only the user file is used, because personal memory reflects the engineer's own working preferences and is applied ahead of repository guidance.
options.C: Both are loaded and their contents combine, with the more specific project file layered over the broader personal one.
options.D: Both are loaded, but the session must be told which one to consult for a given task before either takes effect on its behaviour.

items.question: A biotech company wants a subagent that inspects pull request diffs and reports risks, and it must not be able to modify anything in the working tree. The first version was written with a name, a description, and a system prompt that opens with "You are a read-only reviewer; never edit files." During a trial it edited two files while attempting to demonstrate a fix. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Strengthen the subagent's system prompt with an explicit prohibition repeated at the start and the end, since instruction placement at both ends of a prompt improves adherence.
options.B: Assign the subagent a lower-capability model, which is less inclined to take initiative beyond the task it was given and will therefore stop proposing edits.
options.C: Declare an explicit tool list in the subagent's definition covering only reading and searching, because a definition that omits the tool list inherits the full tool set.
options.D: Add deny rules for the file-editing tools to the repository's shared settings, so no session in this repository can write to the working tree.

items.question: A subagent of the same name exists both in a repository's agents directory and in the engineer's personal agents directory. Which is used in a session opened in that repository?

options.A: Neither, until the collision is resolved; the session reports an ambiguous definition and declines to offer the subagent at all.
options.B: The repository's definition, because project-scoped subagents take precedence over personal ones.
options.C: The personal definition, because configuration closest to the individual running the session always resolves last and therefore wins.
options.D: Both, presented as two separately named entries so the engineer can pick which one to delegate to for a given task.

items.question: Engineers at a travel booking company type a near-identical eight-line prompt several times a day: given a failing test path, read the test, read the code under test, and explain the failure using the team's specific debugging conventions. Everyone has their own slightly different version pasted from a chat thread, and the versions have drifted. The tech lead wants one canonical form, invocable in a couple of keystrokes with the test path supplied at call time.

options.A: Add the eight lines to the repository's memory file so the conventions are always in context and engineers can simply say "debug this test" with the path.
options.B: Publish the canonical text in the team's internal documentation and add a lint rule to the chat bot that flags outdated versions when someone pastes one.
options.C: Create a shell alias that pipes the canonical prompt and the path into a print-mode invocation, and distribute the alias through the team's dotfiles repository.
options.D: Commit a custom slash command in the repository's commands directory containing the canonical text, with the test path substituted from the argument the engineer supplies.

items.question: A retail bank is enabling Claude Code inside its hosted CI workflows. Its cloud security standard forbids long-lived static credentials anywhere in the delivery toolchain, and every workload must obtain short-lived credentials scoped to the job. The bank already consumes Claude through a managed cloud provider under an existing account. How should the workflow authenticate?

options.A: Use the workflow's OIDC identity to federate into the cloud account and assume a short-lived, narrowly scoped role, so no static key is stored in the repository at all.
options.B: Store a long-lived key as an encrypted repository secret, which is masked in logs and only decryptable by the CI system, and rotate it quarterly.
options.C: Store the key as an organisation-level variable rather than a repository secret, so a single rotation covers every repository at once and the exposure surface is reduced.
options.D: Commit an encrypted credential file to the repository and decrypt it at job start with a passphrase supplied from the CI system's secret store.

items.question: A gaming studio's engineers routinely clone third-party and contractor repositories to investigate integration issues. Several of these repositories now ship their own MCP server configuration at project scope. Security has raised that a cloned repository can propose a server that launches a local process or reaches an external endpoint, and that relying on each engineer to evaluate a one-off approval prompt at a moment when they are focused on something else is a weak control. What should the studio do?

options.A: Instruct engineers to open unfamiliar repositories in a session started from a different directory, so the repository's project-scoped configuration is outside the working tree and is never considered.
options.B: Decide centrally which repository-supplied servers may run, expressing that decision in settings the engineer does not control, and leave the per-engineer approval prompt in place as a secondary check.
options.C: Enable the setting that approves all servers found in a repository's project configuration, then rely on the deny rules already in place to restrict what any server's tools can actually do.
options.D: Require engineers to review the repository's project configuration file manually before their first session and to record the review outcome in the studio's ticket system.

items.question: Which hook event can prevent a tool call from executing at all, rather than reacting to it afterwards?

options.A: The post-tool-use event, which receives the tool's result and can suppress it before it is returned to the model.
options.B: The notification event, which fires whenever the session needs attention and can withhold the pending action.
options.C: The pre-tool-use event, which fires before the call runs and can return a decision that denies it.
options.D: The session-start event, which can register a list of calls to refuse for the remainder of the session.
